Chapter 3: How Racism Shapes Institutions and Everyday Life
Most of us don’t start our mornings thinking about how history shapes everything we do. But if you take a closer look, you’ll notice that the rules, traditions, and habits guiding our daily lives are often built on ideas that stretch back generations.
Racism isn’t just about individual attitudes or isolated actions—it's woven deep into the very systems that decide who gets opportunities, who’s protected, and who’s too often left out.
Imagine a family moving to a new city, searching for a good neighborhood and a safe school for their kids. As they explore, they notice some areas are pricier, and the schools there seem to have better resources. When they ask around, they hear those familiar whispers about which neighborhoods are “good” and which ones are “bad.” But here’s the thing—those labels usually line up with race. That’s not just a coincidence. It’s the result of policies and practices set in motion decades ago.
Back in the early 1900s, when cities were growing fast, officials actually drew maps marking certain neighborhoods as risky for investment. These “redlined” areas were most often home to Black families and other minorities. Banks refused to give loans there, making it almost impossible for residents to buy homes or start businesses. Over time, these neighborhoods struggled to keep up, while others thrived.
And today? We still see the impact—wealth gaps, unequal schools, and big differences in opportunity.
Racism shapes far more than just where people live. It influences how folks are treated by police, in hospitals, and at work. Sometimes it’s obvious—like someone being stopped by police for no clear reason, or getting passed over for a job simply because of their name. But often, it’s more subtle. Maybe someone’s overlooked for a promotion, or a doctor ignores a patient’s pain. These patterns aren’t random—they come from rules and habits passed down, often without anyone even noticing.
Even the way history is taught in schools can quietly reinforce what’s unfair. Think about textbooks that focus mainly on the achievements of white leaders, while the struggles and victories of people of color are left out or barely mentioned. That sends a powerful message about whose stories matter and whose are forgotten. For many students, it can feel like their own experiences just don’t count.
But here’s something important to remember—institutions aren’t set in stone. Throughout history, people have come together and demanded change. Sometimes it’s parents organizing for better schools, workers standing up for fair pay, or students walking out of class to protest unfair treatment. These moments prove that systems can be challenged and changed. But it takes courage, and it takes persistence.
It’s easy to feel powerless in the face of problems this big. But every rule, every tradition, started with someone’s choice. And when enough people decide that something isn’t right, they can push for new policies and new ways of doing things.
The first step? It’s seeing how the past continues to shape the present—and refusing to accept unfairness as just “the way things are.”
